stem: Where is the **closing inventory of finished goods** of a manufacturer shown in the year-end statements?

options.content: Income statement cost of sales and current assets
options.rationale: Correct: deducted in cost of sales and shown as a current asset.
Only raw materials and work in progress are adjusted in the manufacturing account.
Finished goods are not in the manufacturing account at all.
Inventory is an asset, never a liability.

explanation: Finished goods inventory is part of cost of sales in the income statement and a current asset in the statement of financial position.

stem: In the income statement of a manufacturer, the production cost of goods completed takes the place of …

options.content: purchases in the cost of sales
options.rationale: Correct: it is the cost of the goods made available for sale.

options.content: revenue at the top of the statement
options.rationale: Revenue comes from sales; production cost is a cost.
It is part of cost of sales, so it is deducted before gross profit.

options.content: closing inventory in the cost of sales
options.rationale: Closing finished goods inventory is still deducted separately.

explanation: Opening finished goods + production cost of goods completed − closing finished goods = cost of sales.

stem: Opening inventory of finished goods US\$11,200; production cost of goods completed US\$96,450; closing inventory of finished goods US\$12,750. What is the cost of sales?

options.rationale: The inventory adjustments are the wrong way round.
The finished goods inventories have been ignored.
Closing inventory must be deducted.

stem: Depreciation of the **office computers** of a manufacturing business is shown …

options.content: as a factory overhead in the manufacturing account
options.rationale: Only factory assets are depreciated as overheads.
Depreciation is never a direct cost here.

options.content: as a deduction from closing work in progress
options.rationale: Work in progress is valued separately.

options.content: as an expense in the income statement
options.rationale: Correct: the computers are used for administration.

explanation: Depreciation follows the asset: office assets to the income statement, factory assets to overheads.

stem: The trial balance shows insurance US\$5,400. US\$600 is prepaid at the year end. Two-thirds of insurance relates to the factory. What is the factory overhead for insurance?

options.rationale: The prepayment has not been deducted.
The whole prepayment has been taken from the factory share only.
This is the office share.

hints: Adjust for the prepayment first, then split.

stem: Which inventories appear as current assets in the statement of financial position of a manufacturer?

options.rationale: Raw materials and work in progress are also owned and unsold.

options.content: Raw materials, work in progress and finished goods
options.rationale: Correct: all three closing inventories are assets.

options.content: Raw materials and finished goods only
options.rationale: Work in progress is also an asset.

options.content: Work in progress and finished goods only
options.rationale: Unused raw materials are also an asset.

explanation: Each closing inventory is listed separately under current assets.

stem: A furniture maker also buys ready-made cushions to sell. Opening finished goods US\$7,300; production cost of goods completed US\$61,850; purchases of finished goods US\$4,150; closing finished goods US\$8,020. What is the cost of sales?

options.rationale: The purchases of finished goods have been left out.
Closing finished goods have not been deducted.
Opening inventory must be added, not deducted.

hints: Bought-in finished goods go straight to cost of sales.

stem: Closing work in progress was overstated by US\$900. What is the effect on the financial statements?

options.content: Profit is understated and current assets overstated by US\$900
options.rationale: A higher closing figure lowers costs, so profit rises.

options.content: Profit and current assets are both overstated by US\$900
options.rationale: Correct: production cost is understated, so cost of sales is too low and profit too high; the asset is too high.

options.content: Prime cost is understated by US\$900
options.rationale: Work in progress is adjusted after prime cost.

options.content: There is no effect on profit
options.rationale: Production cost feeds cost of sales, so profit changes.

explanation: Deducting too much closing work in progress makes the production cost and cost of sales too low, so gross and net profit are overstated; current assets are overstated by the same amount, so the statement still balances.
hints: Follow the error from the manufacturing account to cost of sales.

stem: Carriage outwards of a manufacturer is a factory overhead.
explanation: False. Carriage outwards is a cost of delivering goods to customers, a selling and distribution expense in the income statement.

stem: Accrued factory wages are shown as a current liability in the statement of financial position.
explanation: True. The accrual is added to factory wages in the manufacturing account and shown as other payables (accrued expenses).

stem: A manufacturer's trial balance contains the items below. Match each with the statement where it is used.
explanation: Work in progress and factory depreciation belong to the manufacturing account; finished goods inventory and discount allowed to the income statement; assets at cost and payables to the statement of financial position.

stem: Complete the statement about a manufacturer's cost of sales.

payload.template: Cost of sales is the opening inventory of {{blank:a}}, plus the production cost of goods completed, less the closing inventory of {{blank:b}}.

explanation: The income statement uses finished goods inventories; raw materials and work in progress are dealt with in the manufacturing account.

stem: Electricity paid US\$9,840; US\$360 is owing at the year end. Three-quarters relates to the factory and one-quarter to the office.

payload.template: Factory overheads include electricity of US\$ {{blank:a}} and the income statement includes electricity of US\$ {{blank:b}}.

stem: Revenue US\$154,000; opening finished goods US\$9,600; production cost of goods completed US\$108,250; closing finished goods US\$11,300. Calculate the gross profit.
explanation: Cost of sales 9,600 + 108,250 − 11,300 = 106,550; gross profit 154,000 − 106,550 = 47,450. Ignoring the inventories gives 45,750.
workedSolution: 1. Cost of sales 9,600 + 108,250 − 11,300 = 106,550; gross profit 154,000 − 106,550 = 47,450. Ignoring the inventories gives 45,750.

stem: At 31 December 2025 a manufacturer had: raw materials US\$4,870, work in progress US\$3,150, finished goods US\$9,420, trade receivables US\$15,300 and bank US\$2,860. Calculate the total current assets.
hints: All three inventories are current assets.

stem: Explain why a manufacturer prepares a manufacturing account before the income statement.

points.description: It calculates the production cost of goods completed
This figure is needed for cost of sales / it replaces purchases in the income statement (so gross profit can be found)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The manufacturing account works out the cost of the goods completed in the year. That figure is used instead of purchases in the cost of sales, so the income statement cannot be finished without it.

explanation: The production cost links the two statements.
hints: What figure does the income statement need from it?

stem: Chipo's factory and office share one building. Her bookkeeper charged all the rent to the manufacturing account. Explain the effect on prime cost, on the production cost of goods completed and on profit for the year.

points.description: Prime cost is unaffected (rent is an overhead, not a direct cost)
Production cost of goods completed is overstated by the office share
Profit for the year is unchanged (office expenses understated by the same amount), ignoring any effect on inventory valuation

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Prime cost does not change because rent is an overhead. Factory overheads and so the production cost are too high by the office share of the rent. Office expenses are too low by the same amount, so the profit for the year is the same (unless work in progress or finished goods are valued using the higher cost).

explanation: Gross profit falls but expenses fall by the same amount.
hints: The cost moves from one statement to another.
